figures.caption: Fig. 1: Illustration of two closed-loop evaluation pitfalls. In both panels blue marks the model’s own output: its predicted waypoints and the steering vector they imply. (a) Steering overruling: the red vector is the steering the controller substitutes, aimed at the navigation target point ( red pin). This can mask a model’s failure to compensate its own steering error (left) and can override a maneuver around an obstacle (right). (b) Target-point mismatch: because the evaluation route planner samples the route differently than the planner that collected the training data, the navigation command switches at a different place along the route at test time ( faded red pins) than during training ( red pins). Here the ego receives turn right early and begins to rotate, then receives straight at the junction: the command calls for the straight continuation ( purple ) while its heading and the road geometry support completing the right turn ( green ), a command-context combination absent from training. Interpolating between the two can produce dangerous behavior. SO: steering overruling; TPM: target point mismatch.

Fig. 3: Sample route of SimLingo [ 3 ] , showing driving speed over time together with the cumulative comfort scores of the different implementations. We re-project our distance-based implementation on the time axis. The traditional metric considers driving comfortable when and only when the ego vehicle is standing still, marked by the red shaded bands. Even the slight movement from seconds 35 to 38 is deemed uncomfortable. When we apply our fixes, the metric correctly scores segments when the vehicle is driving comfortably, but still incentivizes standing still. Further applying our distance-based segmentation fixes both problems, not changing the comfort score when the ego vehicle is stationary.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Language2Drive. Language2Drive evaluates autonomous-driving VLA instruction following across four scopes: (A) Atomic actions, (B) Persistent behaviors, (C) Scene-grounded instructions, and (D) Long-horizon programs. To support these task, we build purpose-designed CARLA maps includes cities, underground parking lot, campus and port. We also curate relevant scenarios from AlpSim, NAVSIM, nuScenes, and WOD-E2E. The Task-Coverage chart summarizes the diversity of driving behaviors, while the Word Cloud illustrates the breadth of natural-language expressions. We further introduce the Paired Counterfactual Unit (PCU), which varies the instruction while keeping the driving scene fixed, directly testing whether language changes the vehicle’s behavior. Our benchmark highlights a key distinction: driving competence does not necessarily imply language controllability or reliable instruction following.

Figure 3: Advancement and behavioral response do not establish complete instruction execution. (a,b) P11 requests lane keeping (R0, blue) or a left lane change (R1, orange dashed). Alpamayo 1.5 reaches 100 DrivingScore in both arms but succeeds only on R0. P22 requests 3–7 or 8–12 km/h. Shading marks the requested speed bands, not their active time windows. Curves cover the full post-instruction interval; verification applies from entry into the annotated segment to exit and requires complete traversal and compliance at all active samples. SimLingo passes both criteria; Alpamayo 1.5 passes neither. Figure 9 gives the segment geometry.
